There was something so unusual about Mr. Wopsle’s increasingly intense stare, and he seemed to be puzzling over so many things and becoming so confused, that I could make no sense of it. Long after he had risen into the clouds in an enormous watch case, I remained in my seat thinking about it, still unable to understand. An hour later, when I left the theatre and found him waiting near the entrance, it was still on my mind.

“How are you?” I asked, shaking his hand as we walked down the street together. “I noticed you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he answered. “Yes, naturally I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It’s the strangest thing,” Mr. Wopsle said, slipping back into his bewildered expression, “and yet I could swear it was him.”

Beginning to feel alarmed, I begged him to explain what he meant.

“I can’t say for certain whether I’d have noticed him at first if you hadn’t been there,” he continued in the same distracted manner. “Still, I think I would.”

Without meaning to, I glanced around, as I had grown accustomed to doing on my way home. His mysterious words sent a chill through me.

“Oh, you won’t see him,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He left before I came offstage. I watched him leave.”

With the reasons I had for suspicion, I even began to suspect this poor actor. I wondered whether he was trying to trick me into revealing something. So I looked sideways at him as we walked, but kept silent.

“I had the absurd notion he must have come with you, Mr. Pip, until I realised you had no idea he was sitting behind you there like a ghost.”

The chill returned, but I decided to say nothing yet. His words could easily mean he had been sent to draw me into connecting these remarks with Provis. Of course, I knew with complete certainty that Provis had not been there.

“I expect you find my behaviour surprising, Mr. Pip. In fact, I can see you do. But it’s so extraordinary! You’ll scarcely believe what I’m about to tell you. I could scarcely believe it myself if you told me.”

“Really?” I said.

“Indeed I couldn’t. Mr. Pip, do you remember a Christmas Day long ago, when you were just a child, and I had dinner at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to have handcuffs repaired?”

“I remember it very clearly.”

“And you remember the pursuit of two convicts, and how we joined it? Gargery carried you on his back, and I led the way, and you kept up with me as best you could?”

“So you won’t, will you? What a priceless fool!”

“It’s wicked, isn’t it, Oliver?” asked Charley Bates. “He’ll end up getting scragged, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that word means,” Oliver answered.

“Something like this, old fellow,” Charley said. He grabbed one end of his neckerchief and held it straight up, then let his head fall against his shoulder and forced a strange noise through his teeth. This lively little performance made it clear that getting scragged meant being hanged.

“That’s what it means,” said Charley. “Look at him staring, Jack! I never met such wonderful company as this boy. He’ll be the death of me, I know he will.” After another burst of hearty laughter, Charley returned to his pipe with tears still in his eyes.

“You’ve had a bad upbringing,” the Dodger said, admiring his boots now that Oliver had polished them. “But Fagin will make something of you, or you’ll be the first boy he’s ever taken in who didn’t turn a profit. You might as well begin right away. You’ll be in the business much sooner than you think, and you’re only wasting time, Oliver.”

Charley Bates supported this advice with several moral lectures of his own. When he had finished, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins gave a glowing account of all the pleasures their way of life offered. Throughout it, they dropped hints that Oliver’s best course was to win Fagin’s approval at once, by using the same methods they had used themselves.

“And always remember this, Nolly,” the Dodger said, as they heard the Jewish man unlocking the door upstairs. “If you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the point of talking like that?” Charley interrupted. “He doesn’t understand you.”

“If you don’t steal pocket handkerchiefs and watches,” the Dodger continued, adjusting his language to Oliver’s understanding, “some other fellow will. So the fellows who lose them will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off too. Nobody will be a penny better off except the fellows who take them, and you’ve got just as much right to them as they have.”

“Exactly, exactly!” said the Jewish man, who had entered without Oliver seeing him. “That’s the whole matter in a nutshell, my dear. Take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha, ha, ha! He knows the teachings of his profession.”

The old man rubbed his hands happily as he endorsed the Dodger’s argument, chuckling with pleasure at his pupil’s skill.

The discussion stopped there for the moment. Fagin had brought Miss Betsy home with him, together with a gentleman Oliver had never met, whom the Dodger greeted as Tom Chitling. After lingering on the stairs to exchange a few flirtatious remarks with the lady, the newcomer now appeared.

Among the public edifices of a certain town, which for numerous reasons prudence advises me not to name, and for which I shall invent no name either, stands a building once usual in towns both large and small: namely, a workhouse. In that workhouse there was born, upon a day and date I need not weary myself by specifying, since they can matter nothing to the reader, at this point in our affairs at least, the mortal individual whose name appears at the beginning of this chapter.

For a considerable while after the parish surgeon introduced him to this world of grief and vexation, it remained seriously uncertain whether the infant would live to possess any name whatever. Had he not, these memoirs would most probably never have been published; or, if published, their compass of a page or two would have bestowed upon them the priceless distinction of being the briefest and most accurate biography in the literature of any nation or period.

I do not intend to argue that entering the world in a workhouse is, of itself, the luckiest and most enviable event that can happen to a human creature. I do assert, however, that in this particular case nothing could possibly have served Oliver Twist better. The truth is that Oliver proved exceedingly reluctant to undertake the business of breathing, a tiresome exercise which habit has made indispensable to comfortable existence. For some time he gasped upon a little flock mattress, suspended rather unevenly between this world and the next, with the balance distinctly inclining towards the latter. Had Oliver, during this short interval, been encircled by solicitous grandmothers, nervous aunts, practised nurses, and physicians of immense wisdom, they would certainly and unquestionably have killed him almost immediately. As it happened, no one attended him except an aged pauper woman, somewhat befuddled by an unusual ration of beer, and a parish surgeon who handled such affairs under contract. Oliver and Nature were therefore left to settle the dispute themselves. Consequently, after struggling a few times, Oliver drew breath, sneezed, and announced to the workhouse inhabitants that the parish had acquired a fresh burden. He did so with as powerful a wail as could reasonably be demanded of a male baby whose possession of that highly serviceable accessory, a voice, had scarcely exceeded three minutes and a quarter.
